stimulus.text:
The Corwin Amendment, passed by Congress on March 2, 1861, proposed: “No amendment shall be made to the Constitution which will authorize or give to Congress the power to abolish or interfere, within any State, with the domestic institutions thereof, including that of persons held to labor or service by the laws of said State.”

President James Buchanan, in his annual message to Congress on December 3, 1860, argued: “. . . the election of any one of our fellow citizens to the office of President does not of itself afford just cause for dissolving the Union. . . . secession is neither more nor less than revolution.”

rationales.A: Calling secession revolution denies it is constitutional; revolution stands outside the Constitution.
rationales.B: Buchanan argues no state can lawfully secede; a vote cannot make revolution legal.
rationales.C: By calling secession revolution, Buchanan places it outside the Constitution's lawful remedies. Background: he had just argued at length that the Union was meant to be perpetual, not a rope of sand.
rationales.D: Background: Buchanan held the opposite — that the government had no power to coerce a seceding state.
rationales.general:
1. “Revolution” is Buchanan's verdict, not his praise.
2. A revolution breaks a constitution; it does not use one.
3. Background: Buchanan then claimed the government could not coerce a state back, which left his verdict with no remedy.
4. He condemned secession and then stood aside from stopping it.
Remember: naming an act correctly and acting on the name are two different duties.
